questions.question: A patient has characteristic new pleuritic positional chest pain and elevated CRP. ECG is normal, no rub is heard, and echo shows no effusion. CMR has not been performed. Acute coronary and pulmonary emergencies have been appropriately assessed. Under the ESC 2025 diagnostic-certainty framework, which conclusion is best?
options: Myopericarditis is established by the inflammatory biomarker elevation
Definite pericarditis is already established by pain and CRP
Pericarditis is rejected because ECG and echocardiography are normal
Possible pericarditis; additional assessment can establish greater diagnostic certainty
questions.explanation:
Diagnostic Certainty in Acute Pericarditis

Correct answer: Possible pericarditis; additional assessment can establish greater diagnostic certainty

Count Findings Within the Named Framework

**The compatible presentation is considered separately from the additional diagnostic evidence.** ESC 2025 grades certainty instead of treating all suggestive chest pain as a proven diagnosis.

The additional domains include a pericardial rub, widespread ST elevation or PR depression, CRP elevation, a new or worsening effusion, and imaging evidence of pericardial edema or enhancement.

Do not count one ECG manifestation twice or convert a normal scan into positive evidence. A finding must be credible and interpreted after considering other causes.

Use Uncertainty to Guide the Next Assessment

**Possible disease is a working assessment, not an instruction to dismiss symptoms or prescribe indefinite immunosuppression.** Repeat examination, inflammatory markers and selected CMR can clarify an unresolved presentation.

First exclude a time-sensitive competing cause when indicated. Pericarditic pain can coexist with coronary disease, and an incidental effusion can have a noninflammatory cause.

ACC 2025 also proposes compatible pain or an equivalent presentation plus additional findings, with one additional finding categorized as possible and two or more as definite. This differs from simply reciting the older two-of-four clinical rule. Identify the guideline year in an examination question. Troponin, ventricular function and rhythm answer the separate question of myocardial involvement and risk; a CRP result cannot replace them.

ESC 2025 clinical certainty | Compatible presentation plus

Definite pericarditis | More than one additional criterion

Possible pericarditis | One additional criterion

Unlikely/rejected | No additional criterion; reassess alternatives and the clinical context

Myopericarditis is established by the inflammatory biomarker elevation: CRP indicates inflammation and is not a myocardial-injury biomarker. Myocardial involvement requires appropriate injury evidence, such as troponin elevation and contextual imaging, rather than CRP alone.

Definite pericarditis is already established by pain and CRP: The 2025 framework counts CRP as an additional inflammatory criterion, but a definite clinical diagnosis requires more than one additional criterion beyond the compatible presentation. The supplied evidence provides only one.

Pericarditis is rejected because ECG and echocardiography are normal: A normal ECG and absence of effusion do not exclude pericardial inflammation. These tests provide particular supportive findings rather than obligatory abnormalities in every affected patient.

ESC myocarditis and pericarditis guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192

ACC concise clinical guidance on pericarditis, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.05.023

questions.question: Which imaging modality is usually first line in suspected pericarditis to assess effusion, hemodynamic effects and ventricular function?
options: Transthoracic echocardiography
Contrast-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance
ECG-gated contrast cardiac CT
Transesophageal echocardiography
questions.explanation:
First-Line Echocardiography in Suspected Pericardial Disease

Correct answer: Transthoracic echocardiography

Define What the First Study Must Answer

**TTE assesses the amount and distribution of fluid, chamber function and evidence of impaired filling.** These findings guide immediate triage even though echocardiography does not directly measure every component of inflammation.

Examine several views rather than measuring one echo-free stripe. Document whether an effusion is circumferential or loculated and whether there are concerning chamber-collapse or Doppler findings.

Evaluate both ventricles and regional wall motion. A raised troponin with new ventricular dysfunction changes the concern for associated myocarditis or an alternative ischemic process.

Do Not Confuse a Normal TTE With a Normal Pericardium

**Acute pericarditis can occur without an effusion or visible thickening.** A normal initial TTE therefore does not invalidate a clinical inflammatory presentation.

CMR can demonstrate pericardial edema and enhancement when uncertainty persists or symptoms recur. CT is particularly useful for calcification and extracardiac anatomy; choose it for a specific question rather than as an interchangeable scan.

Reassess promptly if hypotension, increasing breathlessness, syncope or venous congestion develops. A prior small effusion is not protection against subsequent enlargement or rapid accumulation. Conversely, an isolated stable small effusion does not prove active pericarditis. In technically difficult postoperative or regional compression cases, escalate to TEE or appropriate cross-sectional imaging rather than relying on a single reassuring anterior transthoracic view.

Contrast-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance: CMR is especially useful for tissue characterization, uncertainty, recurrence and suspected constriction or myocardial involvement. It does not replace the readily available initial functional and effusion assessment in a straightforward stable first presentation.

ECG-gated contrast cardiac CT: CT defines anatomy, calcification, masses and selected alternative thoracic pathology. It is not the usual initial test for dynamic filling physiology and bedside ventricular assessment.

Transesophageal echocardiography: TEE can identify posterior or loculated collections when transthoracic imaging is inadequate, particularly after surgery. Its semi-invasive nature makes it a selected complementary examination rather than the routine initial study here.

questions.question: A stable patient with recurrent pericarditic pain has normal CRP and an equivocal echocardiogram. Appropriate assessment of competing emergencies is reassuring. The next question is whether active pericardial inflammation is present, and CMR is feasible. Which imaging test is most useful?
options: Cardiac FDG-PET with whole-body assessment
Contrast-enhanced cardiac CT
CMR with edema-sensitive sequences and late gadolinium enhancement
Repeat echocardiography with myocardial strain analysis
questions.explanation:
CMR Evidence of Pericardial Inflammation

Correct answer: CMR with edema-sensitive sequences and late gadolinium enhancement

Separate Edema From Contrast Enhancement

**T2-sensitive edema and pericardial LGE provide complementary information.** Concordant abnormalities can strengthen an inflammatory interpretation when the symptoms and alternative diagnoses fit.

The normal pericardium is thin, so spatial resolution, motion and adjacent fat or fluid can affect interpretation. An apparent bright line must be confirmed on appropriate sequences and views.

Pericardial thickening and effusion add anatomical information but are not required for every active inflammatory episode. CT depicts calcification particularly well, while CMR adds tissue and dynamic functional assessment.

Use Follow-Up Imaging for a Clinical Question

**Residual LGE is not identical to persisting edema or treatment failure.** Enhancement can diminish more slowly than pain or CRP, and prior surgery can complicate its interpretation.

In a patient with normal CRP but recurrent convincing symptoms, imaging may reveal an inflammatory phenotype that a single blood test misses. Conversely, recurrent chest pain without objective evidence warrants reassessment for other causes.

Serial imaging is most useful when it will change treatment, clarify refractory symptoms or assess potentially reversible constriction. Do not prescribe indefinite immunosuppression from one scan or require every mild first episode to undergo repeated CMR. Review ventricular function, myocardial tissue and rhythm separately if myocardial involvement is suspected. The practical aim is to establish the relevant tissue process and monitor an important uncertainty, rather than treating the word enhancement as a diagnosis, pathogen identification or fixed drug indication.

Cardiac FDG-PET with whole-body assessment: PET has selected roles in unresolved inflammatory or malignant disease and can identify extracardiac targets. It is not the usual next test ahead of feasible CMR for focused pericardial tissue characterization in this presentation.

Contrast-enhanced cardiac CT: CT is useful for calcification, detailed anatomy, masses and selected alternative thoracic causes, and can be an alternative when CMR is unavailable or unsuitable. Feasible CMR more directly combines edema-sensitive tissue assessment with pericardial enhancement for this inflammatory-activity question.

Repeat echocardiography with myocardial strain analysis: Repeat echo and strain can clarify ventricular function or associated myocardial involvement. They do not provide the same direct pericardial edema and enhancement assessment when the initial echocardiogram leaves the tissue-activity question unresolved.

questions.question: A patient with a first pericarditis episode has a temperature of 38.7°C, a 24-mm effusion and preserved blood pressure. There is no chamber collapse. Which disposition is most appropriate?
options: Outpatient anti-inflammatory treatment with routine review in two weeks
Hospital assessment with monitoring and a directed search for a specific cause
Immediate pericardiocentesis based on the effusion measurement alone
Outpatient prednisone while awaiting a clinical response
questions.explanation:
Admission and Etiological Evaluation in Acute Pericarditis

Correct answer: Hospital assessment with monitoring and a directed search for a specific cause

Recognize Red Flags Before Hemodynamic Collapse

**Risk assessment concerns both complications and an underlying nonidiopathic cause.** Preserved blood pressure does not erase the significance of a febrile large effusion.

Major red flags include fever ==>38°C==, subacute onset, a large effusion ==>20 mm==, tamponade and failure to respond to aspirin or NSAIDs after at least one week.

Myocardial involvement, immunodepression, trauma and oral anticoagulant treatment are additional contextual concerns. Clinical judgment also accounts for comorbidity, diagnostic uncertainty and access to follow-up.

Investigate According to the Actual Risk

**Admission permits serial hemodynamic assessment and targeted investigation for causes that need specific treatment.** Consider TB, bacterial infection, malignancy and systemic inflammatory disease according to geography, exposure and phenotype.

Obtain baseline ECG, echo, blood counts, inflammatory markers, renal function and appropriate injury biomarkers. Cultures, chest imaging, immune testing and fluid or tissue sampling should answer a clinical hypothesis.

The prospective poor-prognosis study established the importance of fever, a subacute course, large effusion or tamponade and anti-inflammatory treatment failure; contemporary guidance retains these clinical triage principles. Do not turn admission into automatic drainage or an indiscriminate panel of viral antibodies. A patient suitable for outpatient care instead needs an explicit treatment plan, early review and instructions for new breathlessness, syncope or worsening pain. Escalation depends on the evolving syndrome rather than waiting for the full hypotension, muffled-heart-sound and venous-distension triad.

Outpatient anti-inflammatory treatment with routine review in two weeks: Outpatient care is appropriate for uncomplicated low-risk disease with reliable follow-up. Fever above thirty-eight degrees and a large effusion are high-risk features even before hypotension or tamponade develops.

Immediate pericardiocentesis based on the effusion measurement alone: Drainage is urgent for clinical tamponade and can be indicated for suspected purulent disease or important diagnostic or symptomatic reasons. A large measurement alone does not prove tamponade or make every stable patient require immediate puncture.

Outpatient prednisone while awaiting a clinical response: Steroids can treat selected noninfectious causes or refractory disease. Starting them without assessment of this high-risk febrile effusion can obscure a treatable infection and does not provide adequate monitoring.

Prospective study of poor-prognosis indicators in acute pericarditis, 2007 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.106.662114

questions.question: A 27-year-old has a first low-risk pericarditis episode, normal renal function and a reassuring history and examination. There is no large effusion, systemic illness, immunodepression, relevant travel or TB exposure. Which additional etiological testing strategy is most appropriate?
options: Obtain a broad viral antibody panel to identify the causative cardiac virus
Use baseline assessment and reserve further testing for specific clues or an atypical course
Obtain pericardial tissue before classifying the episode as likely idiopathic
Obtain an extensive autoimmune antibody panel before beginning treatment
questions.explanation:
Directed Etiological Testing in Pericarditis

Correct answer: Use baseline assessment and reserve further testing for specific clues or an atypical course

Distinguish a Working Etiology From a Proven Pathogen

**Idiopathic or presumed viral pericarditis is a clinical working category after an appropriate evaluation.** It does not claim that a particular virus has been demonstrated in the pericardium.

History should address infection, TB risk, cancer, kidney disease, medications, immune disease, cardiac injury and recent procedures. Review fever, constitutional symptoms, rash, arthritis and associated pulmonary or neurological findings.

A baseline evaluation still includes ECG, inflammatory and hematological assessment, relevant renal testing and echocardiography. Troponin helps assess possible myocardial involvement when indicated.

Escalate Testing When It Can Change Treatment

**A high-risk feature, recurrence or unexpected treatment failure should reopen the etiological assessment.** The useful investigation is the one that tests a plausible, actionable cause.

For suspected bacterial disease, obtain cultures and appropriate fluid studies rather than a serum viral panel. In possible TB, consider local prevalence, extracardiac sites, fluid microbiology and tissue yield.

A new malignant-appearing effusion, weight loss or a mass changes the imaging and sampling strategy. Systemic inflammatory clues justify focused immune investigation and specialist review. Absence of these features does not justify withholding initial anti-inflammatory treatment until every possible cause has been excluded. Conversely, the label idiopathic must not persist unquestioned when the course becomes febrile, progressive, recurrent or hemodynamically important. Explain this staged approach so reassessment is planned clinical care rather than a claim of absolute etiological certainty.

Obtain a broad viral antibody panel to identify the causative cardiac virus: Seropositivity commonly reflects previous systemic exposure and does not establish pericardial infection. Such a panel rarely changes management of an uncomplicated low-risk presentation.

Obtain pericardial tissue before classifying the episode as likely idiopathic: Biopsy has a role in selected unresolved, recurrent effusive or suspected malignant or infectious disease. Its invasive risk is not justified as a routine etiological requirement in this reassuring first episode.

Obtain an extensive autoimmune antibody panel before beginning treatment: Immune testing is useful when systemic features, a relevant history or an atypical course suggest an autoimmune cause. Unselected broad testing can generate incidental results without identifying the cause of this episode.

  • Idiopathic or presumed viral pericarditis is a clinical working category after an appropriate evaluation. It does not claim that a particular virus has been demonstrated in the pericardium.
    • History should address infection, TB risk, cancer, kidney disease, medications, immune disease, cardiac injury and recent procedures. Review fever, constitutional symptoms, rash, arthritis and associated pulmonary or neurological findings.
    • A baseline evaluation still includes ECG, inflammatory and hematological assessment, relevant renal testing and echocardiography. Troponin helps assess possible myocardial involvement when indicated.

Escalate Testing When It Can Change Treatment

  • A high-risk feature, recurrence or unexpected treatment failure should reopen the etiological assessment. The useful investigation is the one that tests a plausible, actionable cause.
    • For suspected bacterial disease, obtain cultures and appropriate fluid studies rather than a serum viral panel. In possible TB, consider local prevalence, extracardiac sites, fluid microbiology and tissue yield.
    • A new malignant-appearing effusion, weight loss or a mass changes the imaging and sampling strategy. Systemic inflammatory clues justify focused immune investigation and specialist review. Absence of these features does not justify withholding initial anti-inflammatory treatment until every possible cause has been excluded. Conversely, the label idiopathic must not persist unquestioned when the course becomes febrile, progressive, recurrent or hemodynamically important. Explain this staged approach so reassessment is planned clinical care rather than a claim of absolute etiological certainty.

  • A — Obtain a broad viral antibody panel to identify the causative cardiac virus: Seropositivity commonly reflects previous systemic exposure and does not establish pericardial infection. Such a panel rarely changes management of an uncomplicated low-risk presentation.
  • C — Obtain pericardial tissue before classifying the episode as likely idiopathic: Biopsy has a role in selected unresolved, recurrent effusive or suspected malignant or infectious disease. Its invasive risk is not justified as a routine etiological requirement in this reassuring first episode.
  • D — Obtain an extensive autoimmune antibody panel before beginning treatment: Immune testing is useful when systemic features, a relevant history or an atypical course suggest an autoimmune cause. questions.question: A patient meets pericarditis criteria and has elevated troponin. Echo and CMR show preserved regional and global ventricular function, without a new wall-motion abnormality. Which term best describes the conventional pericarditis-predominant overlap phenotype?

Perimyocarditis
Myopericarditis
Inflammatory dilated cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation:
Myopericarditis and Predominant Myocardial Disease

Correct answer: Myopericarditis

Describe the Dominant Clinical Phenotype

**Myopericarditis denotes pericarditis with evidence of myocardial injury but without newly impaired ventricular function in the conventional framework.** Perimyocarditis places greater emphasis on myocardial disease.

The distinction uses imaging and function alongside biomarkers. Troponin concentration alone is not an EF measurement and cannot establish the severity or cause of ventricular impairment.

Contemporary guidance also uses the broader inflammatory myopericardial syndrome framework. The terminology should clarify the actual findings rather than replace a description of function, arrhythmia and hemodynamic status.

Assess Risk and Follow Both Components

**Exclude a relevant ischemic cause and evaluate electrical as well as mechanical risk.** Sustained arrhythmia, advanced AV block or worsening perfusion creates a different care requirement from uncomplicated chest pain.

CMR can characterize myocardial edema and nonischemic injury when clinically indicated. A pericardial LGE line alone is not a myocardial criterion; conversely, preserved EF does not eliminate all myocardial arrhythmic risk.

Treat the dominant pericardial pain/inflammatory syndrome appropriately when there is no HF contraindication, and plan follow-up and exercise advice that account for the myocardial component. Newly reduced EF requires the relevant myocardial-dysfunction pathway and can justify more intensive evaluation. Do not infer that every troponin-positive pericarditis requires an invasive biopsy, empiric antiviral therapy or pulse immunosuppression. The useful examination distinction is injury without new dysfunction versus predominant myocardial disease with functional consequences, followed by risk-based care rather than reassurance from terminology alone.

Myopericarditis | Pericarditis + myocardial injury; no newly impaired LV function

Perimyocarditis | Predominant myocarditis; new ventricular dysfunction may accompany pericardial findings

Isolated pericarditis | No established associated myocardial injury

Isolated acute pericarditis without myocardial injury: An inflammatory marker such as CRP may accompany isolated pericarditis, but the supplied troponin elevation requires assessment of myocardial injury. It cannot simply be omitted from the phenotype description.

Perimyocarditis: This term conventionally describes predominant myocardial involvement, particularly when new ventricular dysfunction accompanies the pericardial syndrome. The supplied preserved function favors the pericarditis-predominant overlap term.

Inflammatory dilated cardiomyopathy: An inflammatory cardiomyopathy involves an appropriate myocardial structural-functional phenotype. Elevated troponin with preserved function in an acute pericardial syndrome does not establish ventricular dilatation or chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

questions.question: An 82-kg adult has a first uncomplicated idiopathic pericarditis episode with persistent pain. Renal and hepatic function are normal, and there is no ulcer history, drug interaction or aspirin/NSAID intolerance. Which initial regimen best fits contemporary first-line treatment?
options: Ibuprofen 600 mg every eight hours with a proton pump inhibitor
Ibuprofen 200 mg every eight hours with colchicine and a proton pump inhibitor
Ibuprofen 600 mg every eight hours with colchicine and a proton pump inhibitor
Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day with colchicine and a proton pump inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Initial Anti-Inflammatory Treatment of Acute Pericarditis

Correct answer: Ibuprofen 600 mg every eight hours with colchicine and a proton pump inhibitor

Prescribe an Anti-Inflammatory Dose, Not Only an Analgesic

**First-line treatment combines aspirin or an NSAID with colchicine.** Add gastroprotection and review renal function, blood pressure, bleeding risk, interacting drugs and the clinical setting.

ESC 2025 reference regimens include aspirin ==750–1000 mg== three times daily or ibuprofen ==600–800 mg== three times daily. Indomethacin ==25–50 mg== three times daily is another anti-inflammatory regimen, often used in incessant or recurrent disease.

Aspirin is preferred with associated ischemic heart disease. Do not combine multiple NSAIDs to compensate for an inadequate response; assess diagnosis, adherence, dose and complications.

Link Duration and Taper to Remission

**The usual initial full-dose aspirin/NSAID period is one to two weeks, with treatment individualized to response.** Maintain adequate treatment until pain and objective inflammatory activity have resolved before tapering.

Reference taper steps are aspirin reductions of ==250 mg== or ibuprofen reductions of ==200 mg== at intervals of one to two weeks, adjusted to clinical response. These are decreases in the dose at each administration, not a new instruction to take the drug once daily.

For this higher-weight patient with normal organ function, a common colchicine regimen is ==0.5 mg== twice daily for the first-episode course. Colchicine reduces recurrence risk and should not be stopped just because pain settles within days. Monitor gastrointestinal intolerance, renal function, blood count and other tests according to exposure and risk. Persistent fever, worsening breathlessness, a growing effusion or nonresponse after an adequate week requires reassessment rather than repeated unsupervised dose escalation.

Drug | Reference adult anti-inflammatory regimen

Aspirin | ==750–1000 mg== orally three times daily

Ibuprofen | ==600–800 mg== orally three times daily

Indomethacin | ==25–50 mg== orally three times daily

Colchicine adjunct | Weight-, organ-function- and interaction-adjusted; first episode generally at least 3 months

Ibuprofen 600 mg every eight hours with a proton pump inhibitor: An appropriate NSAID dose treats pain and inflammation, but omission of colchicine loses an evidence-supported recurrence-prevention component. NSAID without colchicine is selected when colchicine is unsuitable, which this stem excludes.

Ibuprofen 200 mg every eight hours with colchicine and a proton pump inhibitor: This may provide analgesia, but it is below the usual full anti-inflammatory ibuprofen regimen for active pericarditis. Persistent inflammatory pain calls for an adequate anti-inflammatory dose unless patient-specific toxicity limits it.

Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day with colchicine and a proton pump inhibitor: Corticosteroids have a role with specific indications or failure, intolerance or contraindication to first-line treatment. This uncomplicated eligible first episode does not require starting a steroid-based pathway.

The patient receives aspirin and clopidogrel, with no major bleeding or renal contraindication. If anti-inflammatory medication is needed, which strategy is preferred?

Replace aspirin temporarily with an ibuprofen-based anti-inflammatory regimen
Use an aspirin-based anti-inflammatory regimen and consider adjunctive colchicine
Use a prednisone-based regimen as the preferred initial approach
questions.explanation:
Pericarditis After Myocardial Infarction

Correct answer: Use an aspirin-based anti-inflammatory regimen and consider adjunctive colchicine

Reassess New Pain Before Labeling It Inflammatory

**Post-MI pain requires assessment for recurrent ischemia and structural complications.** A positional component and rub support pericarditis but do not independently exclude a second urgent process.

Echo should assess function and effusion. A new large or hemorrhagic effusion, hypotension or an unexpected clinical deterioration raises concern for a mechanical complication rather than an uncomplicated pain syndrome.

Early infarct-associated pericarditis differs in timing from a delayed immune-mediated post-cardiac injury syndrome. Both require the diagnosis to fit the overall course.

Prefer Aspirin When Treatment Is Needed

**The 2025 ACS guideline supports high-dose aspirin for persistent symptomatic early or late post-MI pericarditis and consideration of colchicine.** Its reference aspirin regimen is ==500–1000 mg== every six to eight hours until symptoms improve.

Coordinate the anti-inflammatory dose with the complete antiplatelet regimen, gastrointestinal protection and bleeding risk. Do not add a second aspirin prescription without accounting for what the patient already receives; other P2Y12 regimens can introduce additional prescribing constraints.

The colchicine regimen should be adjusted to weight, organ function and interactions and continued for the appropriate inflammatory course. Evidence specifically dedicated to post-MI pericarditis is more limited than the general acute-pericarditis trial evidence. Nonaspirin NSAIDs and glucocorticoids are potentially harmful after MI because of recurrent ischemic or impaired healing concerns. An asymptomatic effusion by itself does not require routine high-dose aspirin or colchicine. If symptoms persist, reassess diagnosis and complications instead of merely escalating anti-inflammatory exposure.

Use indomethacin as the preferred initial anti-inflammatory agent: Indomethacin can be used in selected nonischemic pericarditis settings. It is not preferred after MI because nonaspirin NSAID exposure can be harmful in this context.

Replace aspirin temporarily with an ibuprofen-based anti-inflammatory regimen: Ibuprofen is a standard option in uncomplicated nonischemic pericarditis. After MI, aspirin is preferred; nonaspirin NSAIDs may adversely affect healing or recurrent ischemic risk and should not replace the antiplatelet plan.

Use a prednisone-based regimen as the preferred initial approach: Corticosteroids are appropriate for selected specific causes or when other treatments cannot be used. They are not the preferred initial post-MI choice because of healing and recurrence concerns.

questions.explanation:
Selecting Corticosteroids for a Specific Pericarditis Setting

Correct answer: Prednisone 0.3 mg/kg/day with colchicine

Identify a Reason to Use Steroids

**A specific immune-mediated cause and an important aspirin/NSAID contraindication can justify corticosteroids.** This is different from starting steroids in every uncomplicated first idiopathic episode.

Colchicine remains useful when it can be given safely. Address the systemic disease with the relevant specialist rather than treating pericardial symptoms as separate from all other lupus activity.

Evaluate infection before immunosuppression, especially TB or bacterial disease when risk or features suggest it. A previous ulcer bleed requires a bleeding and gastroprotection plan rather than assuming any alternative anti-inflammatory is harmless.

Use the Lowest Effective Dose With a Withdrawal Plan

**ESC 2025 lists prednisone ==0.2–0.5 mg/kg/day== as a low-to-moderate starting range for selected pericarditis patients.** Maintain initial treatment until clinical and objective inflammatory remission, then taper gradually.

An initial two-to-four-week reference period does not mean the drug can be stopped abruptly at that point. The full taper often takes longer and must account for recurrence, total exposure and adrenal suppression.

Monitor blood pressure, glucose, infection, weight, mood and bone risk, and provide appropriate prevention for prolonged exposure. Repeated high-dose rescue courses can create steroid dependence while leaving the disease poorly controlled. Persistent or recurrent inflammation despite an adequate plan should trigger reassessment of etiology and consideration of a steroid-sparing strategy matched to the phenotype. The aim is to control a justified indication with a feasible taper, not to regard the fastest short-term pain response as evidence that a higher dose is superior.

Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three days with colchicine: Pulse therapy has roles in life-threatening immune-mediated myocardial or systemic disease. The supplied stable isolated pericardial presentation usually permits an oral low-to-moderate dose strategy.

Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day with colchicine: Higher doses can be needed for specific severe systemic indications. This stable isolated pericardial syndrome is better matched to the lower pericarditis range; higher exposure increases toxicity and can complicate withdrawal.

Azathioprine with colchicine: Azathioprine can be a steroid-sparing treatment for selected systemic or refractory disease. Its delayed effect makes it less suitable than an effective oral glucocorticoid for prompt control of this acute episode.

questions.question: A patient with pericarditis has taken prednisone for several months and is now well on 12.5 mg/day with colchicine. CRP is normal. Previous flares occurred during rapid reductions below 15 mg/day. Which proposed next taper step is most consistent with the ESC 2025 low-dose approach?

Reduce by 2.5 mg/day every week
Reduce by 5 mg/day every two weeks
Reduce by 1.25 mg/day after about four weeks if remission persists

questions.question: Ten days after an uncomplicated isolated pericarditis episode, a runner is pain-free and CRP has normalized. Troponin and ventricular function were normal, and there is no arrhythmia or effusion. The patient requests immediate return to hard interval training. Which plan best reflects ACC 2025 guidance?
options: Return to intense training now after confirming symptom and CRP resolution
Continue exercise restriction for at least one month and confirm remission before a graded return
Resume intense training when the initial two-week NSAID course ends
Continue restriction for six months before reassessing exercise clearance
questions.explanation:
Return to Activity After Isolated Pericarditis

Correct answer: Continue exercise restriction for at least one month and confirm remission before a graded return

Avoid Exercise During Active Pericardial Inflammation

**Exercise advice should incorporate the disease phenotype and objective remission.** ACC 2025 recommends restriction for at least one month after diagnosis or a flare, with activity-related heart rate kept below ==100 beats/min== until remission.

Clinical remission integrates symptoms, examination, inflammatory markers and relevant ECG or echo findings. A normal pain score achieved while taking an analgesic is not by itself proof of resolved inflammation.

The minimum interval is not a guarantee of clearance. Persistent symptoms, effusion, CRP elevation or a more complex course can require longer restriction and additional assessment.

Reintroduce Activity According to the Recovery Assessment

**Isolated pericarditis differs from myocarditis with residual scar or ventricular arrhythmia.** Troponin elevation, new dysfunction, palpitations or syncope should prompt evaluation of an associated myocardial component.

Once the relevant remission criteria are met, use a graded increase and a clear plan for recurrent pain or exercise intolerance. The return decision is separate from the duration of colchicine, which continues to reduce recurrence risk.

Routine repeated CMR until every trace of enhancement disappears is not a universal clearance requirement for a straightforward recovered first episode. Selected imaging is appropriate for an unresolved clinical question, recurrent symptoms or suspected complications. Explain the difference between ordinary low-intensity daily activity and maximal interval or competitive endurance exercise. Review the patient rather than allowing an arbitrary date, the last NSAID tablet or one reassuring laboratory result to serve as the entire clearance assessment.

Return to intense training now after confirming symptom and CRP resolution: Symptom and biomarker recovery are reassuring, but ten days is shorter than the named guidance minimum. Reassess for a graded return after the appropriate restriction and remission assessment.

Resume intense training when the initial two-week NSAID course ends: The drug course and activity restriction answer different clinical questions. Completing a prescription does not independently establish readiness for intense exercise, and the proposed interval is shorter than the named recommendation.

Continue restriction for six months before reassessing exercise clearance: Longer restrictions can be needed with myocardial inflammation, arrhythmia or persistent disease. The supplied isolated uncomplicated pericarditis phenotype does not require applying a high-risk myocardial-disease schedule by default.

questions.question: At 32 weeks of pregnancy, a patient already receiving tolerated colchicine for recurrent pericarditis develops a confirmed inflammatory flare with persistent pain. There is no infection, myocardial dysfunction or hemodynamic compromise. Which added anti-inflammatory strategy is most appropriate through a pregnancy-heart team?
options: Add ibuprofen 600 mg every eight hours
Use the lowest effective prednisone or prednisolone dose while reviewing continued colchicine
Add aspirin 750 mg every eight hours
Add acetaminophen as the sole new treatment for the inflammatory flare
questions.explanation:
Active Pericarditis in Late Pregnancy

Correct answer: Use the lowest effective prednisone or prednisolone dose while reviewing continued colchicine

Match the Drug to Gestational Age

**Late pregnancy changes the aspirin/NSAID balance.** Around twenty weeks onward, NSAIDs can impair fetal renal function and produce oligohydramnios; at approximately thirty weeks and later, premature ductal closure is an additional concern.

FDA advises limiting necessary use between twenty and thirty weeks to the lowest effective dose and shortest duration, and avoiding it from about thirty weeks. These cautions do not mean that all pain or pericardial inflammation should be left untreated.

Low-dose aspirin for an obstetric or vascular indication is a distinct regimen. Do not equate it with the high doses used for acute inflammatory pericarditis.

Preserve Disease Control With a Pregnancy-Compatible Plan

**Prednisone or prednisolone can be used at the minimal effective dose for active pericarditis during pregnancy.** ESC 2025 preferably limits prednisone to up to ==20 mg==/day when feasible; this is a treatment aim, not a reason to leave severe disease uncontrolled. Monitor maternal pressure, glucose and infection risk and plan tapering after remission.

ESC 2025 allows consideration of colchicine during pregnancy, particularly for patients already using it to prevent recurrences. ACR reproductive guidance regards colchicine as compatible throughout pregnancy; it should not be reflexively discontinued solely because of pregnancy.

Review renal and hepatic function, interactions, prior tolerance and the actual inflammatory phenotype before continuing or changing therapy. Lactation decisions require a drug-specific review after delivery rather than assuming every pregnancy restriction persists unchanged. Refractory disease may require specialist discussion of additional therapy, but a generic biologic or cytotoxic prescription is not the next default for this stable flare. Coordinate obstetric and cardiac monitoring and reassess promptly if breathlessness, syncope, hypotension or a growing effusion develops.

Add ibuprofen 600 mg every eight hours: Ibuprofen can treat pericarditis outside pregnancy and in selected earlier-pregnancy settings. At thirty-two weeks, NSAID-related fetal renal and ductal risks make this an unsuitable routine full-dose plan.

Add aspirin 750 mg every eight hours: Anti-inflammatory aspirin doses are different from low-dose obstetric or antiplatelet aspirin. The low-dose safety exception cannot be transferred to this high-dose late-pregnancy regimen.

Add acetaminophen as the sole new treatment for the inflammatory flare: Acetaminophen can provide analgesia in pregnancy. It does not supply the needed anti-inflammatory disease control for the confirmed persistently symptomatic flare described here.

questions.question: A patient has pericarditic pain and objective inflammation continuing for eight weeks after the initial episode. Symptoms have fluctuated, but there has been no remission or symptom-free interval. Which course classification is most appropriate?
options: Recurrent pericarditis
Incessant pericarditis
Chronic pericarditis
A new acute pericarditis episode
questions.explanation:
Recurrent Versus Incessant Pericarditis

Correct answer: Incessant pericarditis

Document Whether Remission Actually Occurred

**The distinction between incessant and recurrent disease depends on the intervening course, not merely the number of pain exacerbations.** Ask about symptom control, inflammatory markers and the treatment timeline.

In the ACC 2025 duration scheme, an acute episode lasts less than roughly four to six weeks, an incessant episode persists beyond that period without remission, and chronic disease lasts more than three months.

A recurrence follows a symptom-free interval of about four to six weeks or longer and should have evidence supporting renewed pericardial inflammation. ESC 2025 frames acute onset as up to four weeks and explicitly includes persistent symptoms or flares during ongoing treatment or drug taper within the incessant course. Its recurrent category requires a symptom-free interval, complete discontinuation of anti-inflammatory treatment and a subsequent supported episode. These distinctions differ from simply counting each on-treatment flare as a new recurrence.

Use the Course to Reassess Management

**An incessant course warrants review of the original diagnosis, cause and adequacy of therapy.** It is not proof of persistent viral replication or an automatic indication for antibiotics.

Review adherence, anti-inflammatory dose, colchicine exposure, steroid initiation and taper, drug intolerance and the possibility of a specific infectious, immune or malignant cause.

Persistent pain alone can have an alternative mechanism. CRP, ECG, echo and selected CMR provide complementary objective information, especially before escalating immunosuppression. Incessant or recurrent disease often needs a longer treatment and taper plan than a straightforward first episode. New effusion, fever, myocardial dysfunction or hemodynamic change requires a fresh risk assessment. Accurate course documentation helps avoid both undertreating continuous inflammation and repeatedly labeling noninflammatory chest pain as a new recurrence.

Conventional/ACC course | Distinguishing feature

Acute | Initial short-duration inflammatory episode; exact boundary depends on the named scheme

Incessant | Persistent activity beyond approximately 4–6 weeks without remission

Recurrent | New supported inflammatory episode after a symptom-free interval of about 4–6 weeks or longer

Chronic | Disease persisting beyond 3 months

Recurrent pericarditis: Recurrence requires a new inflammatory episode after a documented symptom-free interval, conventionally at least four to six weeks. Fluctuation within continuously active disease does not supply that interval.

Chronic pericarditis: The chronic label generally refers to disease lasting more than three months. Eight weeks of continuous activity fits the intermediate incessant course rather than this duration category.

A new acute pericarditis episode: A newly acute event follows the relevant clinical history and time course. Continued inflammation without remission is not reset to a separate acute episode each time the pain becomes more intense.

    • A recurrence follows a symptom-free interval of about four to six weeks or longer and should have evidence supporting renewed pericardial inflammation. These distinctions differ from simply counting each on-treatment flare as a new recurrence.

  • An incessant course warrants review of the original diagnosis, cause and adequacy of therapy. It is not proof of persistent viral replication or an automatic indication for antibiotics.
    • Review adherence, anti-inflammatory dose, colchicine exposure, steroid initiation and taper, drug intolerance and the possibility of a specific infectious, immune or malignant cause.
    • Persistent pain alone can have an alternative mechanism. CRP, ECG, echo and selected CMR provide complementary objective information, especially before escalating immunosuppression. Incessant or recurrent disease often needs a longer treatment and taper plan than a straightforward first episode. Correct answer: Restart full-dose aspirin or an NSAID and use colchicine for at least six months

Common adult regimens with normal clearance include ibuprofen ==600–800 mg== three times daily or aspirin ==750–1000 mg== three times daily, with gastroprotection. For this higher-weight patient, colchicine ==0.5 mg== twice daily is a usual reference regimen.

Continue colchicine for at least six months in recurrent or incessant disease; the final duration can be longer according to remission and recurrence history. Assess interactions and organ function again rather than copying an old prescription without review.

questions.explanation:
An Inflammatory Flare During Prednisone Taper

Correct answer: Add full-dose ibuprofen, maintain colchicine and reassess the prednisone taper

Confirm the Flare and Review What Has Changed

**A documented inflammatory flare during steroid reduction should trigger a treatment review rather than an automatic high-dose steroid cycle.** New pain requires examination and exclusion of another important cause. ESC 2025 includes this on-treatment or taper-associated persistence/flare within its incessant course terminology, rather than requiring it to be called a fully off-treatment recurrence.

Review colchicine adherence, dose, interactions, inflammatory markers and effusion or myocardial findings. Reconsider a specific etiology if the pattern is unexpectedly persistent or progressive.

If an NSAID is suitable, adding adequate aspirin or NSAID treatment can regain control without escalating prednisone. A normal-renal-function adult reference is ibuprofen ==600–800 mg== orally every eight hours with proton pump inhibitor gastroprotection. Continue weight- and clearance-adjusted colchicine, pause further steroid reduction until remission and monitor renal and gastrointestinal safety.

Break the Cycle of Repeated Steroid Rescue

**The vulnerable low-dose range often needs slower tapering after stable remission.** A patient repeatedly flaring at the same dose may need a phenotype-directed steroid-sparing strategy.

IL-1 treatment is evidence-supported in selected refractory inflammatory recurrent disease, particularly with steroid dependence. A single stable flare still requires individualized assessment rather than treating a biologic as the only available next step.

Avoid reducing several effective drugs simultaneously while inflammation remains active. Monitor cumulative steroid harms and possible adrenal suppression and distinguish these from true inflammatory recurrence. Once remission is restored, document the sequence and intervals of withdrawal, with particularly small prednisone reductions below fifteen milligrams daily. Escalating to a severe-disease immunosuppressive regimen is justified by the relevant disease indication, not merely by frustration with a taper. The plan should balance short-term flare control with a feasible route away from chronic steroid exposure.

Increase prednisone to 20 mg/day while continuing colchicine: Restoring steroid exposure can control inflammation when a suitable alternative is unavailable or a specific systemic indication requires it. Here adequate NSAID treatment is still available; using it avoids defaulting to another cycle of increased steroid exposure.

Add azathioprine while continuing the present prednisone taper: Azathioprine can provide longer-term steroid-sparing benefit in selected refractory disease. Its delayed onset does not make it the preferred immediate response to an active flare, and the ongoing taper should be reassessed until remission returns.

Replace the current regimen with daily anakinra: Anakinra is evidence-supported in selected resistant inflammatory recurrent or incessant disease. This supplied stable flare has an available first-line NSAID option and does not establish that adequate conventional treatment has failed.

questions.explanation:
IL-1 Treatment When CRP Is Normal

Correct answer: CMR-supported inflammation can justify considering an IL-1 agent despite a normal CRP

Recognize That Blood and Tissue Findings Are Complementary

**The inflammatory phenotype is not defined by CRP alone.** Credible edema and enhancement can provide objective support when the clinical history and disease course fit.

Exclude alternative chest-pain causes, scan artefact and residual nonactive enhancement. The supplied edema and repeatedly documented inflammatory history make this more persuasive than an isolated incidental LGE finding.

Review ongoing anti-inflammatory exposure, because a measured CRP can be influenced by treatment. A single normal result is not a substitute for longitudinal assessment.

Match Escalation to the Guideline and Patient

**ESC 2025 distinguishes a strong recommendation in resistant recurrent disease with elevated CRP from consideration in selected CMR-inflamed cases regardless of CRP.** The latter is a conditional expert-guidance pathway, not identical trial evidence in every subgroup.

Anakinra blocks the IL-1 receptor; rilonacept is a soluble trap for IL-1α and IL-1β. Adult reference regimens are anakinra ==1–2 mg/kg/day== subcutaneously, maximum ==100 mg==/day, or rilonacept ==320 mg== subcutaneously once followed by ==160 mg== weekly. Review anakinra renal clearance and neutrophil counts, rilonacept lipids, infection risk, vaccination and the drug-specific withdrawal plan. Regulatory indications vary by jurisdiction.

IL-1 therapy can control inflammation and permit corticosteroid withdrawal, but it does not treat every specific infection, malignancy or noninflammatory pain syndrome. Assess TB and other infection risk and review vaccination before initiation. Reassess symptoms, inflammatory activity and relevant imaging after treatment rather than defining success solely by a CRP that was already normal. Do not convert the CRP-normal allowance into a claim that every patient with recurrent pain needs a biologic or that the drug is curative after a fixed number of injections.

Defer IL-1 treatment until a subsequent CRP measurement is elevated: CRP can fail to capture pericardial inflammation, including with treatment or a localized process. The 2025 guidance permits consideration based on convincing CMR inflammation in the relevant resistant clinical setting.

Obtain a pericardial biopsy to document inflammation before considering IL-1 treatment: Biopsy can answer a specific unresolved infectious or malignant etiological question. It is not a routine prerequisite when the established resistant inflammatory phenotype is convincingly supported by CMR as supplied here.

Use azathioprine before IL-1 treatment because CRP is normal: Azathioprine has selected steroid-sparing uses, but it is not an obligatory intermediate step in the named CMR-supported resistant inflammatory setting. Drug choice depends on cause, phenotype, response and safety.

Remission on IL-1 Treatment and Withdrawal Risk

Correct answer: Substantial clinical recurrence despite apparent on-treatment remission

Separate Suppression From Lasting Disease Resolution

questions.question: Using the ESC size convention, a circumferential effusion has a largest relevant end-diastolic echo-free separation of 16 mm. Which size category applies?
options: Moderate
Small
Large
Very large
questions.explanation:
Echocardiographic Effusion Size and Hemodynamic Significance

Correct answer: Moderate

Measure the Effusion With a Defined Method

**Describe both size and distribution.** For the ESC convention, assess the largest relevant echo-free separation at end diastole in an appropriate view rather than adding unrelated measurements.

Small effusions are ==<10 mm==, moderate effusions are ==10–20 mm== and large effusions are ==>20 mm==. Other documents subdivide large and very large collections, so state the named scheme when boundaries are tested.

Use several views to recognize loculation, clot, adjacent pleural fluid and epicardial fat. Serial comparisons should use comparable views and timing; a change in image plane can imitate a change in volume.

Assess Pressure Effects Independently

**Rate of accumulation and pericardial compliance can matter more than total volume.** A rapidly developing small hemopericardium may impair filling more than a slowly accumulating large effusion.

Integrate symptoms, perfusion, pulse and venous findings with chamber collapse, respiratory Doppler changes and IVC assessment. No isolated size threshold replaces the clinical hemodynamic assessment.

The underlying cause also guides action: suspected purulent or malignant disease can require sampling or drainage without overt tamponade, whereas a stable noninflammatory idiopathic collection may be observed. Document the presence or absence of a concerning physiological pattern instead of reporting only a millimeter measurement. A new fall in pressure or worsening dyspnea warrants reassessment even if the previous scan called the effusion moderate. Conversely, normal EF is compatible with tamponade because the primary problem is filling rather than contractility.

ESC echo size | Largest relevant end-diastolic separation

Small | ==<10 mm==

Moderate | ==10–20 mm==

Large | ==>20 mm==

Tamponade | A physiological diagnosis; no single size establishes it

Small: The ESC small category is below ten millimeters. Sixteen millimeters is in the moderate range; preserved EF or blood pressure cannot change the anatomical size category.

Large: The ESC large category is above twenty millimeters. Sixteen millimeters is moderate; the ten-millimeter boundary separates small from moderate, not moderate from large.

Very large: Some other imaging schemes subdivide large collections and use a very-large category above approximately twenty-five millimeters. That subdivision does not describe a sixteen-millimeter effusion in the named ESC scheme.

questions.question: An alert 38-year-old with severe primary hypothyroidism has a stable 24-mm pericardial effusion. There is no chest pain, CRP elevation, chamber collapse or respiratory Doppler evidence of impaired filling. Evaluation finds no competing malignant or infectious cause. Which initial plan is best?
options: Levothyroxine with high-dose ibuprofen and colchicine
Levothyroxine with clinical and echocardiographic surveillance
Levothyroxine with prednisone
Levothyroxine with immediate pericardial drainage
questions.explanation:
A Noninflammatory Effusion in Severe Hypothyroidism

Correct answer: Levothyroxine with clinical and echocardiographic surveillance

Distinguish Fluid Accumulation From Active Pericarditis

**Pericardial effusion is not synonymous with inflammatory pericarditis.** Hypothyroidism can produce gradual fluid accumulation through altered protein handling and lymphatic drainage.

A slow course permits pericardial adaptation, so a sizable collection may occur without classic tamponade. Relative bradycardia can be a clue, but neither bradycardia nor a stable blood pressure independently excludes pressure effects.

Confirm the thyroid biochemical pattern and assess the effusion’s physiology. Continue to investigate if fever, constitutional symptoms, hemorrhagic features or another clue makes an additional cause plausible.

Treat the Cause and Follow the Response

**Levothyroxine is the cause-directed treatment in the supplied stable presentation.** Fluid resolution can take time and should be followed alongside thyroid recovery rather than judged after a few doses.

A usual full-replacement estimate for an otherwise healthy adult is about ==1.6 micrograms/kg/day== orally, individualized to body size and clinical context. Known coronary disease calls for a lower starting dose, commonly ==12.5–25 micrograms/day==, with gradual titration.

Reassess thyroid tests after an appropriate equilibration interval, commonly four to six weeks after a dose change, and adjust according to the relevant thyroid framework. Echo follow-up depends on size, symptoms and trajectory. New hypotension, progressive breathlessness or evidence of impaired filling requires urgent reassessment and possible drainage. Do not transfer this stable outpatient-style thyroid plan to myxedema coma or clinical tamponade, where immediate multisystem and hemodynamic care is required. The correct principle is to identify and treat the noninflammatory cause while maintaining a clear safety and surveillance plan.

Levothyroxine with high-dose ibuprofen and colchicine: Cause-directed thyroid replacement is appropriate, but aspirin/NSAID and colchicine treatment requires an inflammatory indication. The supplied pain-free CRP-negative collection does not establish accompanying inflammatory pericarditis.

Levothyroxine with prednisone: Glucocorticoids can be needed for a separate immune-mediated or adrenal indication. The supplied stable hypothyroid effusion does not establish such an indication or an inflammatory process that requires prednisone.

Levothyroxine with immediate pericardial drainage: Drainage is required for tamponade and can be appropriate for important symptoms or diagnostic concern. The supplied stable adequately investigated collection has none of those indications despite being anatomically large.

questions.question: An asymptomatic patient has a 28-mm circumferential effusion unchanged for six months. A thorough evaluation is unrevealing, CRP is repeatedly normal, and there are no pressure effects or concerning CMR inflammatory findings. Which plan best reflects the revised contemporary approach?
options: A preventive surgical pericardial window
Elective pericardiocentesis with prolonged catheter drainage
Structured surveillance with clinical review and serial echocardiography
An empirical course of prednisone and colchicine
questions.explanation:
A Chronic Large Idiopathic Effusion Without Inflammation

Correct answer: Structured surveillance with clinical review and serial echocardiography

Apply Observation Only After the Relevant Evaluation

**This conservative approach applies to an adequately investigated, clinically stable, noninflammatory phenotype.** It does not apply to suspected bacterial disease, an unresolved malignant concern or impaired filling.

Record size, duration, distribution, symptoms and hemodynamic findings. Reassess thyroid, renal, immune, infectious and malignant possibilities according to the history and course rather than assuming every long-standing effusion is idiopathic.

A normal CRP is one component of the phenotype; persistent symptoms or tissue inflammation can change the interpretation. The supplied patient has repeated reassuring clinical and objective assessments.

Understand Why the Older Drainage Rule Changed

**A prospective cohort of one hundred patients reported a tamponade risk of about ==2.2%== per year, with better recurrence/complication-free outcomes in conservatively managed patients.** This observational evidence informed the newer risk-benefit balance.

The finding is not a randomized proof that drainage is harmful in every patient. Selection and underlying cause matter, and a symptomatic or hemodynamically important effusion remains a different problem.

Arrange a defined review interval, often roughly every three to six months for a stable moderate-to-large collection, adapted to trajectory and access to care. Explain urgent reassessment for new breathlessness, presyncope, hypotension or chest discomfort. Repeat etiological evaluation if the size increases or the phenotype changes. Drainage can be appropriate for evolving symptoms, pressure effects or a management-changing diagnostic question; it is not required solely to make the echo measurement normal. Observation is active follow-up with clear escalation criteria.

A preventive surgical pericardial window: A window can be useful for recurrent symptomatic effusion, selected malignant disease or failed percutaneous management. Its procedural risks are not justified automatically by this stable asymptomatic collection.

Elective pericardiocentesis with prolonged catheter drainage: Older approaches emphasized preventive drainage of chronic large collections. More recent evidence supports observation for carefully evaluated asymptomatic noninflammatory idiopathic cases; persistence and size alone do not establish an intervention requirement.

An empirical course of prednisone and colchicine: Anti-inflammatory treatment requires an inflammatory indication. The supplied repeatedly CRP-negative collection without pericarditis evidence does not establish that the drugs will reduce the fluid.

questions.question: In a high-TB-burden setting, a patient with constitutional symptoms has a lymphocyte-predominant pericardial effusion and fluid ADA of 62 U/L. Initial pericardial-fluid Xpert MTB/RIF is negative. Which diagnostic interpretation is best?
options: TB remains plausible; pursue culture and further targeted confirmation
The negative fluid Xpert excludes active pericardial TB
The ADA result establishes microbiologically definite TB
A positive blood IGRA would establish the effusion as tuberculous
questions.explanation:
Investigating Suspected Tuberculous Pericarditis

Correct answer: TB remains plausible; pursue culture and further targeted confirmation

Distinguish Definite From Supportive Evidence

**Definite TB pericarditis requires appropriate demonstration of TB in pericardial fluid or tissue, by microbiological or relevant molecular methods, or diagnostic tissue evidence.** A supportive biomarker must not be mislabeled as culture confirmation.

Fluid ADA is often interpreted around a 40-U/L threshold in the appropriate lymphocytic clinical setting, but cut-offs and specificity vary. Unstimulated pericardial interferon-gamma can be diagnostically useful where available and is different from a blood IGRA.

Send adequate specimens for mycobacterial culture and drug-resistance assessment as well as the rapid test. A negative smear or Xpert does not make those complementary investigations redundant.

Use the Whole Disease Distribution

**Probable TB can be supported by compatible pericardial disease, TB proven elsewhere and contextual fluid findings.** Search for accessible pulmonary, nodal or other extracardiac sites that can improve diagnostic yield.

Pericardial biopsy may be appropriate when the diagnosis remains unresolved or tissue is needed to distinguish TB, malignancy and other causes. Granulomas require interpretation with microbiology, epidemiology and alternative diagnoses.

Assess HIV status and evaluate for disseminated disease. A clinically unstable effusion needs hemodynamic treatment while diagnostic work proceeds; microbiological completion is not a prerequisite to relieving tamponade. Conversely, a stable patient with weak supporting evidence should not receive an uncritical lifelong TB label from one biomarker. Treatment decisions in a strongly suspected case balance diagnostic probability, the danger of delay, local resistance patterns and the opportunity to obtain useful specimens before therapy.

Finding | Diagnostic role

Positive pericardial culture or appropriate molecular test | Direct etiological evidence; pursue susceptibility information

Lymphocytic fluid with elevated ADA | Supportive, context-dependent; not microbiological confirmation

Unstimulated pericardial interferon-gamma | Useful local biomarker where validated

questions.explanation:
Tuberculous Pericarditis, HIV and Adjunctive Steroids

Correct answer: Standard six-month multidrug TB treatment without routine adjunctive prednisolone

Treat the Infection With a Complete Regimen

**A standard drug-susceptible pericardial-TB course is two months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, then four months of isoniazid and rifampicin.** Adjust to susceptibility, organ function and the applicable TB programme.

Conventional daily adult target doses include isoniazid ==5 mg/kg==, usually maximum ==300 mg==; rifampicin ==10 mg/kg==, usually maximum ==600 mg==; pyrazinamide ==25 mg/kg==; and ethambutol ==15 mg/kg==. Weight-band formulations and local protocols determine the actual dispensed doses.

Monitor hepatic toxicity, ethambutol visual effects, renal dosing and adherence. Provide pyridoxine for appropriate neuropathy-risk patients, including those with HIV, and coordinate rifamycin interactions with antiretroviral treatment.

For Indian programme questions, NTEP uses 2HRZE/4HRE, retaining ethambutol in continuation. Distinguish the named national regimen from the ESC/WHO-style 2HRZE/4HR description rather than silently dropping the programme-specific drug.

Interpret IMPI Without Turning Steroids Into a Universal Rule

**IMPI did not significantly reduce its primary composite of death, tamponade requiring drainage or constriction with adjunctive prednisolone.** It showed reductions in selected secondary outcomes but increased malignancy, particularly HIV-associated cancer.

ESC 2025 considers adjunctive corticosteroids reasonable in selected patients without HIV and advises avoiding them routinely in HIV-infected individuals. This is separate from a distinct indication such as a specifically diagnosed immune-reconstitution complication.

HIV care, infection staging and antiretroviral coordination are essential, but do not substitute for effective TB therapy. Drain an effusion when hemodynamic or diagnostic indications require it and follow for constrictive physiology. A fall in CRP is not proof of sterilization, and an inflammatory complication does not justify shortening the antimicrobial course. Reassess susceptibility, adherence and alternative pathology if the course deteriorates despite treatment. ESC 2025 recommends pericardiectomy assessment if tuberculous pericardial disease is not improving or is deteriorating after four to eight weeks of appropriate TB therapy; do not defer a worsening TB-associated constrictive course solely to complete a generic three-to-six-month noninfectious trial.

Use the four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin pulmonary-TB regimen as the default pericardial regimen: Shorter regimens have defined pulmonary-TB eligibility and supporting trials. Their results should not be automatically extrapolated to this extrapulmonary pericardial presentation.

Standard six-month multidrug TB treatment plus a six-week prednisolone course: Adjunctive steroids can reduce some inflammatory complications, but IMPI did not improve the primary composite and identified an HIV-associated malignancy concern. ESC guidance therefore advises against routine adjunctive use in HIV-infected individuals.

Use two months of four drugs followed by ten months of isoniazid and rifampicin for uncomplicated pericardial disease: Longer courses can be indicated for selected TB sites, resistance or complicated circumstances. Pericardial TB alone does not generally require extending an otherwise appropriate drug-susceptible regimen to twelve months.

questions.question: A septic patient has culture-positive purulent pericarditis. Despite appropriate IV antibiotics and an image-guided catheter, thick loculated material remains poorly drained and compresses the heart. Which source-control strategy is most appropriate?
options: Urgent surgical drainage with loculation disruption and directed IV antibiotics
Continue catheter drainage with image-guided repositioning
Use serial image-guided needle aspirations
Perform balloon pericardiotomy as the preferred next procedure
questions.explanation:
Source Control in Purulent Pericarditis

Correct answer: Urgent surgical drainage with loculation disruption and directed IV antibiotics

Treat a Pericardial Space Infection as a Source-Control Emergency

**Purulent pericarditis requires prompt antimicrobial treatment and adequate drainage.** It is different from treating presumed idiopathic inflammatory pain with an NSAID and colchicine.

Obtain pericardial and blood cultures and assess associated pulmonary, mediastinal, postoperative or bloodstream infection. Include bacterial, anaerobic and fungal considerations according to exposure and immune status.

Begin empirical IV coverage for likely organisms and local resistance patterns while specimens are processed, then narrow to the pathogen and susceptibility. ESC 2025 advises an individualized course until fever and clinical signs resolve, with a minimum duration of three weeks; associated bloodstream or deep infection can require longer treatment.

Choose the Procedure That Can Clear the Actual Collection

**Surgical drainage is indicated when infected material cannot be adequately removed percutaneously.** Direct access permits breaking loculations, removing thick material and maintaining drainage.

Selected intrapericardial fibrinolytic strategies can be considered by experienced teams, but do not use them to postpone necessary surgery when compression or uncontrolled sepsis persists. The supplied failed catheter and thick loculations make complete source control the priority.

Monitor perfusion, organ function, cultures and serial imaging rather than equating a smaller amount of external catheter output with improvement. Residual organization can progress to constrictive disease, so follow-up remains necessary after sepsis resolves. A drainage specimen is also an opportunity to confirm microbiology and identify an unexpected cause; it is not a reason to wait for final culture before stabilizing an infected compressive collection. Steroids or other immune-directed treatment cannot replace antimicrobial therapy and drainage in this setting.

Continue catheter drainage with image-guided repositioning: Image-guided catheter drainage can succeed for a suitable fluid collection. Persistent thick loculated pus causing compression despite inadequate drainage calls for a strategy that can clear the loculations completely, as available with surgical drainage.

Use serial image-guided needle aspirations: Aspiration can provide an initial diagnostic or emergency intervention. Repeated limited aspirations do not reliably clear thick infected loculations and permit ongoing infection and organization.

Perform balloon pericardiotomy as the preferred next procedure: Balloon pericardiotomy has selected roles in recurrent effusions, particularly malignant disease. It is not the preferred way to clear persistent thick infected material requiring direct complete drainage.

questions.question: A patient on maintenance hemodialysis misses several sessions and develops a pericardial rub and a 14-mm effusion. There is no tamponade or evidence of infection, malignancy or another specific cause. Which initial strategy best addresses the likely mechanism?
options: Pericardiocentesis followed by the usual maintenance dialysis schedule
Prednisone with the usual maintenance dialysis schedule
Ibuprofen and colchicine with the usual maintenance dialysis schedule
Intensify hemodialysis with careful ultrafiltration and serial echocardiographic assessment
questions.explanation:
Pericarditis After Missed Dialysis

Correct answer: Intensify hemodialysis with careful ultrafiltration and serial echocardiographic assessment

Identify Inadequate Clearance and Reassess Other Causes

**Pericarditis in kidney failure is not automatically uremic.** Review infection, malignancy, immune disease, medications, infarction and procedure-related complications as appropriate.

The conventional timing distinction places uremic pericarditis before or within roughly eight weeks of dialysis initiation and dialysis-associated disease after that period. Missed or inadequate treatment can create a uremic contribution even in an established dialysis patient.

Assess delivered dialysis, access function, recent interruptions and the clinical trajectory. The usual diffuse ECG pattern may be absent; a normal ECG does not overrule a rub and compatible course.

Intensify Treatment Without Destabilizing Filling

**Frequent dialysis with modest ultrafiltration and serial assessment can treat the cause while avoiding abrupt preload loss.** A published ASN clinical approach uses approximately four-hour sessions daily or six times weekly for seven to fourteen days, individualized to the patient.

Heparin-free dialysis or another appropriate anticoagulation strategy can be considered because hemorrhagic complications are a concern. Use lower ultrafiltration rates when increased pericardial pressure makes filling vulnerable.

Monitor symptoms and repeat focused echo frequently during the initial course; the published approach reassesses about every three days. New pressure effects require drainage rather than continuing a conservative plan through deterioration. An effusion that persists or enlarges despite adequate intensified dialysis also warrants reassessment and possible intervention. Full-dose NSAIDs, steroids and colchicine should not be added reflexively in kidney failure, where benefits and toxicities differ from uncomplicated idiopathic pericarditis. The goal is adequate clearance with maintained perfusion, not simply rapid removal of the largest possible fluid volume.

Pericardiocentesis followed by the usual maintenance dialysis schedule: Drainage is urgent for tamponade and can be needed for enlarging, persistent or important symptomatic effusions. The supplied stable moderate effusion after missed sessions permits initial monitored dialysis intensification.

Prednisone with the usual maintenance dialysis schedule: Steroids can be appropriate for a selected immune or refractory indication. The clear period of underdialysis makes correction of delivered dialysis the initial cause-directed step, rather than adding prednisone without addressing the trigger.

Ibuprofen and colchicine with the usual maintenance dialysis schedule: These drugs treat selected nonuremic inflammatory disease, but do not correct inadequate dialysis. Kidney failure also increases bleeding, residual-function and colchicine-toxicity concerns.

Which strategy offers appropriate durable recurrence control?
options: Radical pericardiectomy
Further image-guided needle aspiration when symptoms recur
A pericardial window integrated with the oncological treatment plan
Repeat catheter drainage with intrapericardial sclerosis
questions.explanation:
Recurrent Malignant Pericardial Effusion

Correct answer: A pericardial window integrated with the oncological treatment plan

Confirm the Cause Rather Than Inferring It From Cancer History

**An effusion in a patient with cancer is not necessarily malignant.** Infection, radiation, treatment-related inflammation, renal disease and other causes remain possible.

Cytology with an appropriate cell block is important when fluid is sampled; selected tissue investigation can improve an unresolved assessment. A negative cytology result does not exclude every malignant effusion.

Assess hemodynamic urgency, recurrence pattern, loculation, performance status, prognosis and patient goals. Clinical tamponade requires relief regardless of the later recurrence-control choice.

Match Recurrence Control to Benefit and Burden

**A surgical window can provide sustained drainage after recurrent symptomatic collections.** It is one option alongside prolonged catheter drainage, selected balloon procedures and disease-specific oncological strategies.

The appropriate procedure depends on anatomy, local expertise, prior response and goals. A short expected survival or major procedural burden can favor a less invasive palliative plan rather than the same operation for every patient.

Systemic cancer treatment may control the underlying process but cannot be relied on to relieve an acutely compressive collection immediately. Selected intrapericardial therapies are used in specific cancers and centers, with a distinct risk-benefit assessment. Continue to monitor for reaccumulation, drain complications and constrictive consequences. Do not interpret a technically successful window as control of the malignancy itself. Explain the practical aim—fewer recurrent symptomatic collections—and distinguish that from an unsupported survival claim or a need to remove the entire pericardium.

Radical pericardiectomy: Pericardiectomy is used principally for important constrictive disease and selected refractory situations. Its greater operative burden is not the routine first surgical solution for recurrent malignant fluid when a drainage window can address the problem.

Further image-guided needle aspiration when symptoms recur: Aspiration can relieve an accessible collection or suit selected palliative goals. This repeatedly recurrent pocket lacks a safe percutaneous route, so a durable surgical strategy is better matched to the anatomy and clinical course.

Repeat catheter drainage with intrapericardial sclerosis: Catheter-based prolonged drainage and selected intrapericardial therapies can reduce malignant-effusion recurrence when access is suitable. The supplied unsafe percutaneous route prevents treating that as the preferred practical strategy here.
